lines.cap: **Narrator:** Room 8H. Monday. Period 3. Mr Hargreaves is on mug number fourteen.
**Mr H:** Term 2 portfolio. Write an original **identity poem**, plus a **commentary** explaining your craft.
**Mei:** Easy! 'My culture is big and sometimes I'm **sad**. Feeling confused is really quite **bad**.'
**Nib:** I have leaked onto the mark book. 'Sad' and 'bad'? Darling, my nib is weeping.
**Cliché:** Ooh, I LOVE it! Add '**tears like rain**' and '**a heart of gold**'! Never fails!
**Mei:** Why is a sparkly greeting card talking to me?
**Rex:** Silence, greeting card! Replace 'rain' with **pluvial precipitation**! Replace 'sad' with **lugubrious**!
**Narrator:** Thesaurus Rex has just eaten Mei's notebook. Nobody else in 8H has blinked.
**Will:** Give her back her parchment, thou overgrown dictionary! Writing a poem requires **soul**!
**Mei:** Writing poetry: **one star**. My homework is inside a dinosaur.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode nine: Show, Don't Haiku.
**Narrator:** Six p.m. Queenstown. Mei is staring at the word 'IDENTITY' in capital letters.
**Mei:** I don't have a giant tragic identity! I have curry puffs and homework!
**Ah Ma:** Mei-ah! Rice cooker just clicked! Come and fold dumplings before the skin dries out!
**Mr H:** Stop starting with big **abstract nouns** like 'culture' or 'belonging'. Start with **things**.
**Nib:** Remember **Old Photos Make Sounds**: **Objects**, **Places**, **Memories**, and **Sounds** of home.
**Mei:** Like George Ella Lyon's '**I am from**' list! 'I am from the click of the rice cooker...'
**Mr H:** Generate a whole page, then **narrow your focus** to **one** object, **one** afternoon, **one** kitchen.
**Nib:** Climb down the **ladder of abstraction**! 'Culture' is abstract: you cannot photograph it.
**Mei:** Down to **concrete nouns**: Ah Ma's **jade bangle**, her **floury thumb** pinching each dumpling fold!
**Mr H:** Golden rule: **show, don't tell**. Give the reader the **thing** that causes the feeling.
**Will:** Emily Dickinson wrote: '"**Hope**" is the thing with **feathers**.' Abstract idea, concrete bird. Exquisite.
**Cliché:** Or say Ah Ma is **as warm as toast** with a **rich tapestry of cultures**!
**Nib:** Shoo! Test every image with **SEE it, OWN it, PIN it**. Sensory, uniquely yours, and **precise**.
**Mei:** Not 'flower' — **frangipani**. Not 'a language' — **Hokkien**. Two stars!
**Narrator:** Tuesday. The library. The SILENCE PLEASE sign has grown a new sticky note.
**Mr H:** **Form** is a poem's overall shape and rules. **Structure** is how ideas develop inside it.
**Mei:** I'm picking **free verse**! No regular metre, no rhyme scheme, so anything goes!
**Nib:** Incorrect, darling! Free verse is **not** 'anything goes'. Without rhyme, every **line break** carries the shape.
**Mr H:** You could use a **list poem** with **anaphora**: repeating 'I am from' to build a chant.
**Nib:** Or a **dramatic monologue**: one persona speaking to a silent listener, even an object like a suitcase!
**Will:** Or the **sonnet**! **Fourteen lines** of **iambic pentameter**! My Sonnet 18: three quatrains and a rhyming **couplet**!
**Nib:** Whereas a **Petrarchan sonnet** splits into an **octave** of eight lines and a **sestet** of six, turning at the **volta** on line nine.
**Mei:** What about a **haiku**? Five, seven, five syllables and I'm done by lunch!
**Mr H:** A real haiku captures one **present moment**, with a season word, **kigo**, and a cutting dash, **kireji**. No explaining.
**Nib:** A **ghazal** uses couplets ending in the same **radif** after a rhyming **qafia**, with the poet's name, **takhallus**, at the end.
**Mei:** Wait — the **pantoum** comes from the Malay **pantun**! Right here in our region!
**Mr H:** **Two and four go forth**: lines **2 and 4** of each quatrain become lines **1 and 3** of the next, looping like memory.
**Mei:** A pantoum for Ah Ma's kitchen — repeating like folding dumplings! Okay, that's cool.
**Narrator:** Wednesday. Kevin is practising standing at the end of a line without panicking.
**Kevin:** When punctuation finishes a line, it's **end-stopped**! Firm! Safe! Nobody falls off!
**Nib:** When a sentence runs over the line break without punctuation, that is **enjambment**.
**Mr H:** Look: 'a suitcase that is **never** / quite unpacked.' The last word of a line gets the **spotlight**.
**Mei:** For a split second, '**never**' sounds permanent — until 'quite' softens it on the next line!
**Will:** In Edward Thomas's Adlestrop, the train 'drew up there / **Unwontedly**.' The line halts just like the train!
**Kevin:** And after 'Unwontedly.' is a **caesura** — a pause **mid-line**! I'm creating stillness! I'm helping!
**Nib:** **Stanza** is Italian for '**room**'. Never end a line on weak words like 'the' or 'and' by accident.
**Cliché:** Now add rhyme! 'My grandmother is very **wise**, she always bakes her apple **pies**!'
**Nib:** **Forced rhyme**! Twisted word order like 'to market we did go', filler words, and pies Ah Ma has never baked!
**Mr H:** Read aloud for **sound**, not just rhyme: **alliteration** in Tennyson's 'clasps the crag with crooked hands'.
**Will:** **Sibilance** and soft 'm' sounds in Keats's 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness'. Plus **assonance**, **plosives** and **onomatopoeia**!
**Mei:** And if full rhyme sounds sing-song, use **half-rhyme** like 'kept' and 'slipped', or none at all. Three stars!
**Narrator:** Thursday. Mei is on Draft Two. Thesaurus Rex has broken into her bedroom.
**Rex:** Why write 'Uncle Lim's wok roars' when you can write 'the culinary cauldron **vociferates**'?!
**Mr H:** Out, Rex. Good poets don't stuff big words in — they **redraft** until every plain, concrete word earns its place.
**Mei:** Wait, don't real poets write a masterpiece in one flash of pure inspiration?
**Nib:** Elizabeth Bishop wrote seventeen drafts! Follow the loop: **Generate, Shape, Cut, Sharpen, Listen, Rest**.
**Mei:** Draft One: 'I have two passports, I feel **confused**, / Two different countries, I am **bemused**.' Yikes.
**Mei:** Draft Three: 'two passports in a drawer, / one blue, one red, / the same boy in both / **trying hard not to blink**.'
**Mr H:** You cut the forced rhyme, swapped abstract feelings for concrete colour, and **showed** the pressure.
**Will:** And 'Uncle Lim's wok **roars** like a small jet'! Onomatopoeia! Even I am hungry!
**Nib:** Never call it 'Untitled'. Make your **title** work: name the form, echo a phrase, or add context.
**Cliché:** And end with: 'And that is why we should all respect every culture!'
**Mr H:** Never end with a **moral summary**. End on a **resonant image** or a quiet turn.
**Mei:** In my dumpling pantoum, 'It falls apart' changes in the last stanza to: '**I try again. It holds this time.**'
**Mr H:** Keep both drafts. Your commentary needs the before and after.
**Narrator:** Friday. The poem is finished. Now comes the three-hundred-to-six-hundred-word commentary.
**Mei:** So I just summarise what my poem is about and say I used enjambment to make it flow?
**Nib:** 'Make it flow'?! Summary earns pennies! A commentary analyses **your choices** like a critic, in the **first person**!
**Mr H:** Six steps: **I Invent Fresh Tunes, Rewrite, Evaluate**. **Intentions, Influences, Form, Techniques, Rewrite, Evaluate**.
**Mei:** For **Influences**, I name the exact poem: like Sujata Bhatt's '**it blossoms out of my mouth**', I left Hokkien untranslated!
**Kevin:** When you quote your own poem, put a **slash** to show a line break! Don't forget the slash!
**Nib:** And use **tentative phrasing** about the reader: 'I **hoped** this **might suggest**', never 'the reader will definitely cry'.
**Mei:** Let's climb PEEL! **Point**: I used sound imagery in stanza one to show unspoken family worry.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: 'my grandmother's jade bangle / **tapping** the table like a **question** / she never quite asks.'
**Mei:** **Explain**: Onomatopoeia in 'tapping' and enjambment after 'question' let the reader hear her quiet fear I'm losing Hokkien.
**Mei:** **Link**: And **Evaluate** honestly — stanza three is looser, so next time I'd cut the flip-flops line.
**Mr H:** Specific self-quotation, precise effect, and an honest weakness. That... is top band.
**Narrator:** Before portfolio hand-in, the English department would like to save you some marks.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! **Old Photos Make Sounds** for ideas; **SEE it, OWN it, PIN it** for images; **Two and four go forth** for a pantoum.
**Nib:** And for the commentary: **I Invent Fresh Tunes, Rewrite, Evaluate**.
**Mr H:** One. Don't **tell** feelings with abstract nouns like 'sadness'. **Show** them with concrete objects and actions.
**Cliché:** Two. Avoid **forced rhymes** and worn-out **clichés**. Apparently 'tears like rain' is banned now. Rude.
**Kevin:** Three. Don't break lines randomly on 'the' or 'and'. Every **line break** needs a job you can explain!
**Rex:** Four. Precise concrete nouns beat **thesaurus stuffing**. Even if 'pluvial precipitation' is magnificent.
**Will:** Five. Never end your poem with a **moral summary**. End on an **image** that lingers.
**Nib:** Six. In your **commentary**, quote yourself with slashes, explain **effects**, show a **redraft**, and **evaluate** honestly.
**Ah Ma:** Mei! Your dumpling holds its shape today! And the poem is not bad, lah!
**Mei:** Ah Ma said 'not bad'! That's basically a Nobel Prize! Writing poetry: **four stars**.
**Will:** Four?! You wrote a pantoum!
**Mei:** Seventeen drafts is a lot of work, Will.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Should an identity poem build mainly on **abstract nouns** or **concrete nouns**?
**Mei:** **Concrete nouns**: things the reader can see, hear, smell or touch.
**Mr H:** In a **pantoum**, which two lines of each stanza become lines 1 and 3 of the next?
**Will:** **Lines 2 and 4**. Two and four go forth!
**Mr H:** What do we call it when a sentence runs over a **line break** without punctuation?
**Nib:** **Enjambment**.
**Mr H:** How do you mark a **line break** when quoting your own poem inside your commentary?
**Kevin:** With a forward **slash**, surrounded by spaces!
**Mr H:** What six parts belong in a commentary: **I Invent Fresh Tunes, Rewrite, Evaluate**?
**Mei:** **Intentions, Influences, Form, Techniques, Redrafting, and Evaluation**.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Writing Poetry & Commentary** quiz in your English Lab.
**Rex:** May I eat Cliché now?
**Cliché:** Catch me if you can, greenosaurus!
**Mr H:** Not in Room 8H.
